title: How did the Barkley Marathons start? The story behind the world's toughest ultramarathon
claims: The first Barkley Marathons took place in 1986 and was named after Gary Cantrell's neighbour and friend Barry Barkley.
The first editions covered about 50-55 miles with about 25,000 feet of climbing, and the course was extended in 1989.
The modern format is five loops of about 20 miles within 60 hours, described by Cantrell as 100 miles, while some claim the real distance is closer to 130 miles.
No GPS is allowed, so the true distance of the course cannot be measured by runners.
The 2026 edition started on 14 February, the earliest start by a wide margin, while the race is usually held in March or early April.
The event is held in Frozen Head State Park, a 24,000 acre park with 14 peaks between 1,340 ft and 3,000 ft and very few roads or man-made structures.
The article states that of approximately 1,000 runners who have started, only 20 people have finished the Barkley Marathons.
The article quotes Frozen Ed Furtaw, the first finisher, writing in 1996 that Barkley is intentionally set up to minimise the number of finishers while staying within the limits of possibility.
Since 2017 runners are given an analogue watch set to 00:00 at the start instead of the real time.
The route is altered every year and there is no website and no route map.
Entry is not published: runners have to work out when and where to send an essay along with a 1.60 US dollar entry fee, and first-time runners must bring a number plate from their home town.
The article states that Jasmin Paris became the first woman to complete the Barkley Marathons in 2024.
The article describes the Barkley as having no GPS, no waymarks and no aid stations, with checkpoints marked only by books from which runners tear a page.
The article states that a sombre rendition of Taps is played each time a runner drops out.
The article lists route section nicknames including Danger Dave's Climbing Wall, Leonard's ButtSlide, Rat Jaw and Testicle Spectacle.
The article states that a finisher's total climb and descent over five loops is equivalent to going up and down Mount Everest twice.
